Yelloweye rockfish (Sebastes ruberrimus) attain a relatively large body size among northeastern Pacific rockfishes, with field surveys and morphometric studies indicating that the maximum recorded total length for this species is 104 centimeters [Li = 104 centimeters]. This considerable ultimate length, which is achieved only by the oldest individuals, reflects a protracted period of somatic growth that spans many decades in the cold, productive waters of the Gulf of Alaska and British Columbia. The asymptotic size is accompanied by a substantial adult body mass; based on length-weight regressions derived from fishery-independent surveys, a fish at ultimate size carries a wet weight of approximately 17,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 17,000 grams]. This value places Sebastes ruberrimus among the most massive of the Sebastes genus, a status that is consistent with its position as a long-lived, slow-growing apex predator in rocky reef and shelf environments. The energetic costs of attaining and sustaining such a large body are considerable, and the species allocates its resources toward structural growth for many years before the onset of reproductive investment.

The onset of sexual maturation in Yelloweye rockfish occurs at a body size considerably smaller than the ultimate maximum, reflecting a life-history strategy common among long-lived scorpaeniform fishes. Puberty is attained at a total length of 40 centimeters [Lp = 40 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to a wet weight of 892 grams [Wwp = 892 grams] as estimated from the same length-weight relationship used for adults. This weight at maturation is several orders of magnitude greater than the mass at the earliest life stages, highlighting the substantial somatic investment required before reproductive physiology becomes active. Individuals of Sebastes ruberrimus that have reached this size are considered subadults, with gonadal recrudescence initiating during the late winter months prior to the summer spawning season. The length-based schedule of maturity is broadly consistent across the species' range, though local variation in growth rates driven by temperature and food availability can shift the precise age at which this 40-centimeter length is achieved, with slower-growing populations in colder waters taking additional years to reach pubertal size.

Reproductive output in Yelloweye rockfish is among the highest recorded for viviparous marine teleosts, a direct consequence of the species' large body size and its strategy of producing a single, high-fecundity brood annually. At a water temperature of 5.7 °C [T = 5.7 °C], a typical thermal condition for this species during the peak spawning period in subarctic waters, females release approximately 2.7 million larvae per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 2.7 million larvae per spawning event] through a single spawning event each year [F_R_i = single spawning event each year]. This annual reproductive rate is underpinned by the efficient packing of small, yolk-rich oocytes within the large ovaries of gravid females. The larvae, which are extruded as free-swimming individuals following internal fertilization and embryonic development, begin exogenous feeding almost immediately after parturition. The high fecundity is an adaptation to the intense pelagic mortality that characterizes the early larval phase, with only a tiny fraction of the larvae surviving to settle onto suitable rocky reef habitat many weeks later.

At the very onset of life, as yolk-sac larvae emerge following internal gestation, the mass of each individual is remarkably small. Each larva weighs a mere 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams] immediately following parturition, a mass that is derived from the small egg diameter of approximately 0.8 millimeters. This diminutive initial wet weight, which is reflective of a viviparous reproductive mode that produces large numbers of tiny, undeveloped offspring, stands in stark contrast to the massive final adult body mass. The larvae are initially lecithotrophic, relying on endogenous yolk reserves for their first few days of life, and they begin active feeding on planktonic prey shortly after yolk-sac resorption. The vast disparity between the newborn mass and the ultimate adult mass, spanning nearly eight orders of magnitude, underscores the extraordinary scope of the growth trajectory and the prolonged period of feeding and energy acquisition required to complete the species' life cycle. Pelagic larvae drift with ocean currents during this vulnerable stage, gradually developing fins and other juvenile characteristics before settling to the benthos.

Longevity is a defining feature of the life history of Yelloweye rockfish, which is renowned as one of the longest-lived of all marine fishes. At a water temperature of 5.7 °C [T = 5.7 °C], a temperature that reflects the mean annual conditions of their deep reef habitat, the maximum recorded lifespan is 118 years [am = 118 years]. This extreme longevity, which far exceeds that of most other vertebrates, is enabled by a combination of factors including low metabolic rates in cold water, delayed senescence, and a habitat structure that offers ample refuge from predation for large adults. The oldest individuals, often exceeding 100 centimeters in length, provide crucial demographic stability to the population, contributing to multiple spawning events over many decades. Such a long life span necessitates very slow natural mortality rates among adults, a demographic pattern that makes the species particularly vulnerable to overfishing. The combination of slow growth, late maturation, and extreme longevity classifies Sebastes ruberrimus as a typical K-selected species, with population recovery times measured in decades following any significant reduction in adult abundance.
